talks.title: The AppSec Hallway Track: RSAC 2026 | StackHawk + Semgrep
talks.teaser: Booth-floor insights on how AI-driven code growth strains AppSec teams, how to win budget, and why hands-on AI practice matters.
talks.summary:
Scott Gerlach of StackHawk and Kyle Northcutt of Semgrep share what CISOs and booth visitors told them at the show. The core problem is code velocity: teams ship far more code while AppSec headcount stays flat, against a long-cited ratio of about one AppSec person to 100 developers. Non-engineers now build apps too, so sending a vulnerability ticket to the original author fails. The proposed fix is to run scans inside the build, where an agent triggers a Semgrep or StackHawk scan, reads the output and fixes issues before release.

On budget, the speakers suggest tying AppSec funding to the company's push to accelerate with AI, arguing for money to make that speed secure instead of funding measured by ticket volume. Teams must weigh what to buy from partners versus build, and they need architecture and guardrails so AI-built work stays repeatable rather than collapsing after a few weeks. Security staff should sit with engineering to see its agentic process and find where AppSec fits.

Their advice is to get hands-on with coding agents even if you are skeptical, because knowing where authentication and authorization break is hard from theory alone. Kyle described a weekend project building an MCP server for an espresso machine, which taught him the strengths and weaknesses of both the tool and the model. Leaders should ask engineers questions and allow time for lab experiments, since attackers have the same tools and asset management and testing cadence must keep pace.

talks.title: Liminal Demo Day's - Application Security in the Age of AI
talks.teaser: Shows how API discovery, pipeline scanning and deterministic findings fit into a shared security and engineering workflow.
talks.summary:
Scott Gerlock, co-founder and chief security officer at StackHawk, presents an approach to API and application security testing built into the development lifecycle. AI agents and fast DevOps let teams ship code so quickly that attack surface grows faster than security can track. He says about 30% of customer code repositories become attack surface, and manual discovery can take about a year, while the platform does it in roughly 15 minutes.

The platform connects to source code repositories, flags newly built APIs and their engineers, and reports commit activity and sensitive data such as PII, PCI and PHI. It also generates OpenAPI specs from code. A portable scanner runs inside a company's network on CI/CD runners. In a pull request demo, a high-severity finding broke the build and appeared in the PR with the affected path, request, response and a curl command to reproduce it. He argued AI can help plan tests while pass-or-fail results stay deterministic.

Business logic tests for broken object and function level access can run in QA and production environments, while injection tests belong earlier in the lifecycle. An overview shows how much attack surface is under test and how often it is tested, with alerts when testing slips past a one- or two-week window. In the Q&A, he said security teams usually open the conversation, and some customers feed findings to coding agents to fix. His takeaway is that security, engineering and AI teams need shared oversight.

talks.title: Reimagining Application Security for the AI Era
talks.teaser: Explains how security teams can track and test new APIs and applications as AI speeds up code creation.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the claim that software teams now write code much faster than before, and that people who never shipped production code are doing so too. The speaker argues that this growth puts more code into production than people fully understand, and cites a figure that AI-generated code carries about 20% more vulnerabilities than human-written code. That gap gives attackers more room to exploit a fast-moving attack surface.

The presenter then describes how StackHawk approaches the problem. The product analyses source code to show security teams which APIs and applications are being added, including those created with AI, and surfaces them in near real time so security can work with engineering on testing. Because application security teams have limited resources, the aim is to help them decide where effort will reduce risk most. The second part moves runtime application and API testing into the software development lifecycle, so developers can find and fix flaws before release.

A case study from ITV, a broadcaster that runs the public-facing ITVX streaming service, shows the approach in use. Public endpoints such as user profile endpoints draw hostile attention, so the team wanted visibility into what was exposed. According to the speaker, the tooling surfaced vulnerabilities much earlier in the development cycle and put findings in front of the people who had to act on them. The closing message is that security needs to move closer to the code and use automation to keep pace with AI-driven change.

talks.title: What is API Security Testing? How to Get Started
talks.teaser: Introduces API security testing and outlines the steps for starting with automated scans in CI/CD.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a survey figure: 99% of organizations saw API security issues in the past year, and more than half delayed releases because of them. It explains that APIs are now a prime target because they expose business logic and data directly, with no user interface in front of them. API security testing finds weaknesses in endpoints, authentication and authorization before attackers exploit them, and it has shifted from a periodic task to automated runs in CI/CD on every pull request.

Tools read API specifications, and sometimes source code, then send crafted requests aimed at specific flaws. One example logs in as one user and tries to reach another user's records to test broken authorization; another sends malicious payloads to probe for injection. The talk compares testing types: dynamic testing runs against the live application and proves what is exploitable, though it is the strongest fit for APIs. Static analysis scans code early but yields more false positives, software composition analysis flags known vulnerable dependencies, and penetration testing adds human experts who look for novel attack paths.

Getting started follows a sequence. Inventory every API, including REST, GraphQL, gRPC and internal microservices, then keep accurate OpenAPI or GraphQL schemas. Pilot one representative API and expect some tuning. Add scans to CI/CD with plugins for GitHub Actions, GitLab or Jenkins, running on pull requests, and set up remediation workflows so findings get fixed. The speaker says catching a vulnerability during development costs 100x less than fixing it in production.

talks.title: DAST vs Penetration Testing: Which Security Testing Method is Best?
talks.teaser: Weighs DAST against penetration testing on speed, cost, coverage and accuracy, and argues for using both.
talks.summary:
This short explainer asks whether teams should choose dynamic application security testing (DAST) or penetration testing, and argues that the best answer is often both. It describes DAST as automated checking of a running application from the outside. It sends hostile inputs without any view of the source code, and modern versions run inside CI/CD pipelines for ongoing feedback. Penetration testing, by contrast, combines automated tools with human testers who think like attackers, chain flaws together, and judge real business impact.

The comparison covers five areas. DAST returns results in minutes to hours and can run on every build, while a pen test takes one to three weeks and usually recurs quarterly or yearly. DAST carries low running costs once it is set up, whereas a pen test is quoted at $15k to $100k per engagement. DAST scales to hundreds of applications with little extra effort, but its coverage is broad and shallow and generic attack patterns can produce false positives. Human testers filter those out and reach complex logic flaws. The talk suggests DAST suits continuous testing and fast developer feedback, while pen testing suits high-value applications, compliance obligations and multi-step attack scenarios.

The closing point is that the two methods are complementary. DAST supplies automation and breadth through continuous testing, and pen testing supplies depth at critical milestones. Used together, they give a fuller picture of security coverage.

talks.title: SAST vs DAST: Stop Choosing, Start Correlating
talks.teaser: Correlating static and dynamic application security findings cuts duplicate triage and sharpens remediation priorities.
talks.summary:
Many application security programs treat static analysis and dynamic scanning as an either-or choice, even though each addresses different parts of the risk picture. Static application security testing inspects source before build, surfacing insecure patterns and common weakness categories early when fixes are cheaper, but it cannot fully judge runtime behavior and tends to produce more noise. Dynamic testing attacks the running application with realistic inputs, confirming exploitability for issues such as SQL injection while catching authentication and business-logic flaws that static tools miss, at the cost of later timing and heavier setup.

The friction appears when both tools run without alignment. The same flaw can spawn separate tickets, leaving engineers to reconcile duplicates and sending developers conflicting priorities. The presentation cites teams spending roughly 40 to 60 percent of effort on overlapping triage instead of closing real gaps.

The recommended shift is correlation rather than consolidation into one modality. Linked findings merge code location from static results with runtime confirmation from dynamic tests, so queues reflect true exploitability, developers receive direct fix context, and fixes can be validated through the full lifecycle as one tracked item. Practitioners should treat the pair as complementary coverage and invest in connecting signals to prioritize verified risk and accelerate remediation.

talks.title: REST API Security Best Practices
talks.teaser: Covers core REST API defenses: token authentication, limiting data exposure, input validation, and gateway-level controls.
talks.summary:
The video opens by noting that REST APIs are stateless and built on standard HTTP methods, which makes them popular and also an attractive target. It then works through its recommended practices in turn, starting with token-based authentication, typically using JWTs or OAuth 2.0 tokens. Tokens should be short-lived, sent only over HTTPS, and paired with refresh flows and revocation so compromised credentials can be cut off quickly. Identity, permissions and expiry claims should be checked on every request.

The second practice concerns what responses expose. Filtering fields by user role, using serialization layers that strip sensitive values, and reviewing responses for internal IDs, system paths, verbose errors or personal data are all covered. The same section stresses strict input validation for types, formats and ranges, plus sanitizing content before processing. OpenAPI schema checks are presented as a useful first layer that supplements, rather than replaces, application-level validation.

The final practice is to centralize controls in an API gateway. Rate limiting and throttling at the gateway help against abuse and denial-of-service attempts, while consistent TLS, authentication and access policies can apply to every endpoint. Gateway logging of authentication attempts and authorization failures supports both real-time alerting and later investigation. Cloud-native gateways such as AWS API Gateway are named as options, with the advice to pick one that fits the infrastructure and configure it securely.

talks.title: GraphQL Security Best Practices
talks.teaser: Covers five practices for securing GraphQL APIs, from query limits and introspection control to field-level authorization.
talks.summary:
This short video walks through five practices for securing GraphQL APIs, framed around the way GraphQL lets clients shape their own queries. The first two focus on limiting what a single request can cost. Query depth and complexity limits stop deeply nested queries from exhausting server resources, with complexity scores assigned to fields and expensive queries rejected before execution. Batching controls cap how many operations a client can pack into one HTTP call, and rate limiting should count individual operations rather than requests so batching cannot be used to get around it.

The next practices concern exposure and access. Introspection should be disabled in production, or restricted to authenticated users, with introspection queries logged to spot reconnaissance. Interactive tools such as GraphiQL should also be kept out of production. Field-level authorization means checking permissions in each resolver that returns sensitive data, using declarative rules where possible and considering the path a query took to reach a given field.

The final practice is auditing every route to sensitive data, including indirect ones, and enforcing authorization at each resolver regardless of how the query arrived. The speaker recommends automated testing to discover query combinations, since manual review can miss authorization bypasses. The takeaway is that GraphQL needs controls built for its architecture, not only endpoint-level checks.

talks.title: What Is Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)?
talks.teaser: Explains how live-app scanners simulate attacks to find exploitable flaws and where they complement static code review.
talks.summary:
Passing security unit tests and green builds do not guarantee that a deployed application will withstand realistic abuse. The session introduces dynamic application security testing as validation against running software: tools send request patterns that mimic attackers, then interpret responses to flag problems such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and authentication bypass without requiring source access.

Coverage walks through how scanners map attack surface using HTML spiders, OpenAPI for REST, GraphQL introspection, and AJAX crawlers for single-page apps, then exercise each endpoint with crafted payloads. DAST is compared to static analysis—blueprints versus stress-testing the built system—and positioned as complementary. Reported strengths include fewer false positives because alerts tie to demonstrable exploitability, visibility into runtime-only defects including business logic gaps, and independence from language or framework. Practical guidance favors pre-production targets to limit data corruption, CI/CD automation on each build, and API-first support across REST, GraphQL, and gRPC with remediation routed into developer workflows.

The conclusion argues that mature programs pair static and dynamic testing so runtime risk is checked before production. It also notes that newer commercial offerings aim to broaden surface mapping and embed continuous feedback in pull requests, while the core takeaway remains early, actionable fixes during development.

talks.title: gRPC Security Best Practices
talks.teaser: Outlines five practices for securing gRPC microservices, from protobuf schema validation to mutual TLS and service mesh monitoring.
talks.summary:
This short StackHawk video presents five security practices for gRPC services. The presenter explains that the efficiency and interconnectedness that make gRPC useful also widen the attack surface between services. The first practice is to use Protocol Buffer definitions to validate incoming messages against precise types, required fields and valid ranges, and to add application-level input checks, since a message that matches its schema may still be unsafe.

The second practice applies least privilege between services, so each one can call only the methods it needs, with authorization checks on specific operations rather than just connection rights. This limits lateral movement if one service is compromised. The third practice is mutual TLS, where client and server authenticate each other before data is exchanged, with Application Layer Transport Security noted as an option inside Google's infrastructure. The fourth layers transport security with token-based message authentication using OAuth 2.0, JWT bearer tokens or OpenID Connect, so each request needs valid credentials.

The final practice is logging and monitoring of gRPC calls, tracking which services call which endpoints, how often and with what data, and watching for unexpected calls, high request volumes or failed authentication attempts. These records support both detecting active attacks and building audit trails after an incident. The video closes with a recap of the five practices and a pointer to StackHawk's website.

talks.title: OWASP Top 10: Essential Web Application Security Risks to Know (2025)
talks.teaser: Walks through the ten most common OWASP web application risks, from broken access control to server-side request forgery.
talks.summary:
The video opens by noting that AI tools are speeding up developers in 2025, which widens the attack surface. It introduces the OWASP Top 10 as the standard list of common web application threats and walks through each category. Broken access control covers apps that fail to limit what signed-in users can reach, such as URL tampering or unauthorized API calls. Cryptographic failures cover weak encryption, poor key handling and unprotected data.

Injection means malicious input slipped through user fields, with SQL injection, cross-site scripting and AI prompt injection given as examples. Insecure design describes flaws from rushed architecture that patching cannot fix. Security misconfiguration includes default production credentials, exposed cloud buckets and loose CORS policies. Outdated components are libraries with known flaws, a risk the video ties to AI-accelerated coding. Authentication failures let attackers compromise passwords, sessions or identities. Integrity failures cover supply chain attacks and unauthorized pipeline changes. Logging and monitoring gaps let intruders go unnoticed. SSRF tricks a server into reaching internal systems, possibly exposing cloud metadata.

The presenter says the biggest threat depends on the application, though access control, cryptographic failures and injection usually top the list. The takeaway is to build security into development from the start: map the attack surface from source code, run automated tests in CI/CD pipelines, and give developers actionable feedback. A linked article covers mitigations.

talks.title: How to Use the StackHawk MCP Server in Claude Code
talks.teaser: Walks through wiring StackHawk's MCP server into Claude Code for live scans, agent-driven fixes, and iterative retesting before production.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the point that AI-assisted coding does not guarantee secure output, and positions the StackHawk MCP server as a way to test applications while developers work in Claude Code. The walkthrough covers StackHawk account setup, application creation, API key generation, and adding the MCP server via the Claude MCP JSON command with global, project, or team-wide scope options. The speaker confirms registration by listing MCP servers, inspecting the generated Claude configuration, and using slash-MCP in Claude Code to view available StackHawk tools.

A sample prompt asks the agent to scan the project using an existing StackHawk YAML file or create a StackHawk project if needed. The live scan returns several findings, including a medium-risk CSP wildcard directive and lower-severity issues such as missing permission-policy and X-Content-Type-Options headers and an X-Powered-By leak. No high-severity items appear in the demo, but the workflow still treats the results as worth fixing.

The agent applies remediations and re-runs scans when issues persist, illustrating a loop that continues until remaining problems are resolved. Practitioners should leave with a concrete pattern: connect StackHawk through MCP, trigger scans from natural-language prompts inside the IDE, and use repeated scan-and-fix cycles to harden code before release.

talks.title: How to Use the StackHawk MCP Server with Windsurf
talks.teaser: Shows how to connect the StackHawk MCP server to Windsurf so Cascade can run scans and list vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
This short tutorial shows how to connect the StackHawk MCP server to Windsurf, so that StackHawk scanning can be driven from Cascade, Windsurf's coding agent. The walkthrough starts in the Windsurf settings, where the MCP servers section is opened from Cascade and the raw MCP configuration file is edited to add the StackHawk entry.

The server needs a StackHawk API key. The presenter creates one under an existing StackHawk application, names it for Windsurf, and places it directly in the config file for simplicity, noting that an environment variable could be used instead. After saving the file and refreshing the MCP list, the StackHawk server appears as available in Cascade.

To test the setup, the presenter asks Cascade to scan the code with the StackHawk server. Cascade runs the scan using the configuration already in the project, and the resulting vulnerabilities are listed in the side panel. Cascade can then be asked to fix those findings and retest them through the same MCP server. The takeaway is that scan, fix and retest can happen inside an AI coding agent workflow, with setup details pointed to the StackHawk website.

talks.title: How to Use the StackHawk MCP Server in Cursor
talks.teaser: Shows how to connect the StackHawk MCP server to Cursor so its agent can run security scans in chat.
talks.summary:
The tutorial walks through connecting the StackHawk MCP server to the Cursor editor so that its agent can work with StackHawk directly from the chat window. The presenter starts in a project that already uses StackHawk and has an application registered in the StackHawk platform, which is the setup the integration builds on.

Connection is done from Cursor's settings, under the MCP and integrations area, where a custom MCP server is added. The configuration launches the server through uvx and needs a StackHawk API key. The presenter creates a new key in StackHawk's API key settings, labels it for Cursor, and places it straight into the config for simplicity, noting that an environment variable is an alternative. Once saved, StackHawk appears in the MCP tools list, which shows which tools are available to the chat.

To confirm it works, the presenter asks the agent in chat to scan the project for security vulnerabilities using StackHawk. The scan then runs through the MCP server from inside the conversation, and a run option for the scan is also shown in the corner of the chat. The takeaway for practitioners is that a StackHawk scan can be triggered from an AI coding assistant as part of everyday development, once the server is configured with a valid key.

talks.title: API Discovery Feature: Sensitive Data Identification Office Hours
talks.teaser: Shows how automated source-code review surfaces PII, PHI, and PCI in APIs so teams can rank endpoints for security testing.
talks.summary:
Organizations often lack a reliable picture of which APIs exist and which ones matter most. The session opens on an awareness gap: modern applications depend on APIs as the primary attack path, yet teams frequently prioritize testing from tribal knowledge, spreadsheets, or gateway traffic that only sees live endpoints. Those approaches miss shadow or idle APIs, drift as code ships faster—especially with assisted development—and make it hard to report risk to leadership or support incident response and compliance.

The core announcement is sensitive data identification inside API discovery. Rather than inferring risk only from traffic, the workflow analyzes connected repositories to find APIs and classify code that handles regulated categories—PII, PHI, and PCI—with matched variable names, severity hints, and filters in an attack-surface view tied to development activity such as recent commits. The walkthrough explains why source control is treated as the source of truth, support for major Git platforms and multiple languages, and continuous reanalysis as code changes.

Practitioners should take away a prioritization model: combine existence, change rate, and sensitive-data signals to decide what to test next, reduce guesswork compared to monitoring alone, and improve audit confidence with testing history on high-risk endpoints. The hosts note customer-reported gains in coverage and describe the capability as built into discovery without extra agents, then invite questions on how audiences currently solve the problem.

talks.title: Office Hours: Obliterate Security Bugs with StackHawk and Github
talks.teaser: Explains how StackHawk's dynamic testing and GitHub's code scanning combine to catch exploitable web and API bugs in pull requests.
talks.summary:
The webinar explains how StackHawk and GitHub work together to catch security bugs early in the development lifecycle. The presenters compare three testing approaches: software composition analysis, which flags known-vulnerable dependencies; static analysis with CodeQL, which flags risky code patterns; and dynamic testing, which attacks a running application. Dynamic findings come with evidence of exploitation but no source location, so the presenters argue that correlating them with static results gives the full picture.

Next the speakers walk through the GitHub integrations. API discovery scans connected repositories for web applications and APIs that need testing, which exposes coverage gaps. A GitHub Actions step runs the application on the build agent and scans it there, usually in about five to ten minutes. Results appear as pull request comments and in the GitHub security dashboard, and a severity threshold can fail the check when new high-severity issues appear.

The live demo follows a sample Java Spring application whose pull request fails on high-severity SQL injection findings. The evidence view shows the malicious request, the database error returned, and a generated curl command for reproducing the attack. The correlated CodeQL result points the developer to the vulnerable line. The session closes by contrasting StackHawk with Burp Suite, which suits manual testing more than pipeline automation, and with Trivy, which focuses on dependency scanning.

talks.title: GitHub and StackHawk Office Hours: Code to Runtime Application Security
talks.teaser: GitHub and StackHawk Office Hours: Code to Runtime Application Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this office hours session, the StackHawk team—featuring Morgan, Scott, Brian, and April—explores how integrating StackHawk's dynamic application security testing (DAST) with GitHub and GitHub Advanced Security (GHAS) bridges the gap between code-level development and runtime security. Rather than treating application security as a reactive, firefighting exercise after code reaches production, the presentation outlines how teams can proactively find and fix API and web application vulnerabilities directly within their continuous integration and continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines.

### Key Topics
- **Complementary Security Testing Models (SCA, SAST, and DAST):** The speakers contrast Dependabot (software composition analysis / SCA) and CodeQL (static application security testing / SAST) with StackHawk (DAST). Dependabot flags known vulnerable third-party dependencies (CVEs), while CodeQL identifies vulnerable patterns and code smells in static source code with precise line-of-code tracking, though it can generate false positives. StackHawk tests running applications, validating exploitability in runtime with low false positives.
- **AI-Powered API Discovery:** StackHawk connects directly to GitHub repositories as a source of truth. It analyzes codebases, detects frameworks, commit frequency, and recent committers, and catalogs web applications, APIs, GraphQL, and gRPC endpoints to provide visibility into attack surfaces and track testing coverage.
- **GitHub Actions & Pull Request Checks:** Using the official HawkScan action, teams can execute automated dynamic scans against ephemeral preview environments or local application instances in CI/CD. Test results and breaking vulnerabilities (based on OWASP severity ratings) are commented directly into pull requests.
- **Unified Security Dashboards via Updated SARIF:** StackHawk worked with GitHub and Microsoft to update the SARIF standard, enabling DAST findings to publish alongside static findings directly in the GitHub Advanced Security code scanning dashboard.
- **SAST and DAST Correlation:** StackHawk matches dynamic findings to static CodeQL findings using Common Weakness Enumeration mappings (such as CWE-89 for SQL injection). This pairs runtime proof of exploitability with the exact line of code requiring remediation.

### Technical Details
During the live demonstration, April showcases a Node.js Express application (`Vuln Node Express`) configured with a GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/HawkScan.yml`). The workflow installs Node.js, installs dependencies, runs unit tests, boots the application locally in the background, and runs `HawkScan` using API credentials, branch name, and commit SHA. The scan is configured to generate SARIF artifacts and fail builds when high-severity vulnerabilities are detected. In the demo, StackHawk flags high-severity SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) issues on the `/search` endpoint. By integrating with CodeQL via GitHub APIs and matching CWE-89, the platform reveals curl-reproducible runtime request/response evidence alongside the exact file and line (`search.js`, line 6).

### Takeaways
Deploying developer-friendly DAST in pre-production pipelines eliminates the overhead of managing IAST/RASP agents and allows teams to test without interference from production mitigations such as rate limiters. By surfacing actionable, curl-reproducible proof in pull request comments and linking dynamic exploits to static code lines, organizations can efficiently prioritize remediation, reduce dashboard fatigue, and deploy secure software rapidly across microservices and cloud environments.

talks.title: The API Security Problem No One is Talking About
talks.teaser: Argues that discovering APIs from source code and testing them before production beats relying on production traffic monitoring.
talks.summary:
The webinar, given by two co-founders of a dynamic application security testing vendor, argues that many security teams cannot say which APIs their organisation runs. Faster releases and AI code assistants add APIs quickly, and the speakers cite 70% of internet traffic as API driven.

The speakers contrast production monitoring with true discovery. Monitoring can flag attacks, but it is reactive, expensive, hard to trace back to code, and blind to services that never receive traffic, which creates survivorship bias. They illustrate that with the wartime bomber armour story. Instead, they describe discovering APIs from source code repositories, with large language models recognising APIs even without an OpenAPI spec. In their customer data at least 30% of repositories held APIs needing testing, most customers added about one new repository a day, and a thousand repositories were processed in about 15 minutes.

Their takeaway is to find APIs early, test them directly before production in CI/CD, and give developers findings while code is being written. Production monitoring still has value but should not be the only control.

talks.title: Constructing a Secure AppSec Foundation with CommunityAmerica Credit Union & StackHawk
talks.teaser: Constructing a Secure AppSec Foundation with CommunityAmerica Credit Union & StackHawk.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this webinar, Lake Setzer (Information Security Lead at CommunityAmerica Credit Union) and Scott Gerlock (CSO and Co-founder at StackHawk), hosted by Alexa Sevilla, discuss the transformation of CommunityAmerica's Application Security (AppSec) program. In early 2021, CommunityAmerica made a strategic pivot from purchasing third-party applications to developing in-house software, prompting the rapid creation of an internal AppSec program. Initially, the program adopted traditional, centralized tooling that failed due to misaligned licensing models, slow external scanners, and an inability to handle modern microservice architectures and specific frameworks like Micronaut for Java. The discussion chronicles how Lake shifted his approach from centralized control to developer enablement and cross-functional partnership, adopting modern SAST, SCA, and DAST tooling integrated directly into CI/CD pipelines.

### Key Topics
- **Initial AppSec Failures and Lessons Learned**: Early tooling relied on legacy point-and-click scanning and per-application pricing models that proved unsustainable for hundreds of microservice repositories. Scanners suffered from pipeline delays and failed to analyze Micronaut frameworks.
- **AppSec Shift-Left Maturity Model**: Evaluating an organization's maturity from stage 1 (centralized control, audit-driven scanning) toward stages 3 and 4 (shared ownership, developer-driven scanning, and automated proactive gates).
- **Developer & Cross-Team Partnership**: Aligning with key engineering teams—specifically the Enterprise Integration Platforms (EIP) team, the digital frontend team, and devops—by actively listening, accommodating their workflows, and eliminating development bottlenecks.
- **Tooling Selection & Architecture**: Evaluating tools based on framework compatibility, simultaneous scanning, developer-focused licensing, and fast execution inside CI/CD pipelines.
- **Business Alignment & Risk Defense**: Framing AppSec not merely around vulnerability tallies, but around brand reputation, member trust, and core organizational assets.

### Technical Details
CommunityAmerica supports approximately 50 developers across five major teams working within a polyrepo environment containing hundreds of microservices. To support their architecture, the AppSec tooling stack was revamped:
- **SAST & Code Quality**: SonarQube was selected to provide static analysis, enforce code formatting guidelines (such as PEP 8 guidelines for Python), and detect standard security issues.
- **SCA**: Snyk was integrated to manage software composition analysis and open-source dependency vulnerabilities, compensating for framework-specific limitations and lack of native SCA in SonarQube.
- **DAST**: StackHawk was chosen for dynamic API and application security testing. Key requirements included rapid scan times (regularly completing under two minutes or even under one minute), unlimited scans across environments (development, testing, and production) without extra licensing penalties, and the ability to run directly inside CI/CD pipelines and local developer environments.
- **Pipeline Integration**: Scans trigger automatically on build and pull request events using Jenkins and Azure Repos. Scan results decorate pull requests directly, giving developers immediate feedback on passes or failures.
- **Policy & Gates**: The team established automated triage criteria where high, critical, or urgent vulnerabilities (levels 3, 4, and 5 on a 5-point scale) require mandatory remediation, moving gradually from soft gates to hard build/PR blocking gates.

### Takeaways
- **Ditch Centralized Control**: AppSec teams cannot act as the sole bottleneck; success requires stepping back from centralized control and co-owning security with developers.
- **Listen and Solve Engineering Problems**: Security professionals must actively consult engineering and devops teams, understand their operational hurdles, and provide tooling that speeds up development rather than stopping releases at the last minute.
- **Target High-Impact Teams First**: Rather than attempting a sweeping organization-wide rollout, partner first with high-code-volume teams (such as platform/EIP teams) to test, iterate, and build a reusable model for other groups.
- **Automate to Eliminate Noise**: Automation in triage and pipeline feedback reduces manual handoffs and prevents vulnerability backlogs from ballooning, turning security findings into incremental, lint-like fixes.

talks.teaser: Explains why traditional DAST falls short for APIs and how modern dynamic API testing fits into CI/CD workflows.
talks.summary: StackHawk CSO Scott Gerlach argues legacy DAST fails on production-only, black-box scans with neutered payloads and no API semantics, while modern dynamic API testing belongs in pre-production CI with OpenAPI-driven gray-box attacks covering most OWASP API Top 10 items via real request-response probes. He contrasts iast and runtime API tools’ traffic dependencies, urges autogenerated OpenAPI specs, HAR-derived tests when specs are missing, and seed realistic parameter values to avoid 500-heavy brute forcing.

talks.title: Elevate Your AppSec Program with the Dynamic Duo: StackHawk and Snyk
talks.teaser: Participants see how SAST and DAST correlation in StackHawk surfaces exploitable flaws and links them to source for faster fixes.
talks.summary:
The session frames application security as a paired static-and-dynamic testing story. Presenters describe Snyk’s scanners across first-party code, open-source dependencies, containers, and infrastructure-as-code, plus integrations that meet developers in IDEs, source control, and CI/CD pipelines. They argue static analysis gives broad coverage and fix guidance but can be noisy and may not prove exploitability, while dynamic testing exercises live applications for issues such as injection and cross-site scripting but does not point to exact source lines. Correlating both on shared weakness identifiers is presented as the way to prioritize, reproduce, and remediate faster.

A platform walkthrough follows a billing service through staging and test environments. Hawk Scan results show severity breakdowns, plugin coverage, and a SQL injection finding with request and response evidence, validation via curl, and linked Snyk Code entries that jump to the vulnerable line. Audience questions cover discovery without HAR files, path coverage reporting, authentication options, custom active and passive scripts, and scanning many microservices as separate applications.

A StackHawk engineer describes internal “champagne” dogfooding and a weekly operations review where the team inspects observability, dependency, static, and dynamic findings together. Snyk’s speaker closes with continuous testing, fix-focused workflows, runtime context for prioritization, IDE education links, and automated checks from commit through deployment. The through-line for practitioners is embedding automated, developer-owned security rituals rather than periodic checkbox assessments.

talks.title: How to Shift Left the Right Way
talks.teaser: Outlines how organizations align people, process, and tools so developers can fix application security issues earlier.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing shift-left application security as a journey to put testing into developer workflows, then argues that fixing flaws is usually harder than finding them. Security and engineering see different slices of each application, lack a shared language for severity, and often split finders from fixers, which produces interrupt-driven work and weak SLA-driven deferrals.

Speakers trace how agile, distributed teams, infrastructure-as-code, cloud, serverless, and AI-assisted coding accelerated releases and widened what must be reviewed. They describe benefits such as proactive prevention, stronger engineering champions, and prioritizing security work like test coverage rather than chasing zero defects. Organizational change needs people, process, and technology advanced together—not buying tools alone—with feedback from engaged development partners, clearer roles (including a RAPID-style decider often in development leadership), and buy-in so rollouts avoid silent vetoes.

On execution, they contrast CVSS-heavy backlogs with EPSS-style exploit likelihood, focus process on the common middle of the portfolio, and stress developer-usable automation, noise reduction, and correlated static plus dynamic signals in pull requests. A brief demo shows StackHawk and Snyk checks failing a GitHub pull request with fix guidance in the developer flow. The close repeats that appsec is a business delivery problem with no silver-bullet tooling.

talks.title: Turning Win-don’ts into Win-do’ws: Automating HawkScan Across Azure Pipelines, Windows, and More
talks.teaser: Walks through running the HawkScan API scanner on Windows and Azure Pipelines, including NTLM logins and proxy certificates.
talks.summary:
This StackHawk office-hours session covers running the HawkScan API scanner on Windows and inside Azure Pipelines. The presenters explain that HawkScan is released as a Docker image, a zip archive and a Windows MSI installer, and that the MSI bundles its own Java runtime. A live command-line install shows the MSI being fetched and placed on the path without manual edits. The zip option is presented as the better fit when a team restricts the MSI service or PowerShell scripts.

The middle of the session walks through a pipeline example using the Azure Marketplace extension tasks, which install the scanner and run it against a sample Spring application in a build matrix across Windows and Ubuntu. The web application has to be started within the same pipeline before the scan begins. For self-hosted Windows runners, the speakers note that disabling the MSI service or PowerShell execution rules out the matching installer type. A separate demo shows NTLM authentication configured in the YAML file, with logged-in and logged-out indicators, so the scan can get past pages that return a 401 response.

The final demo covers a transparent proxy that breaks Java's certificate validation. Instead of importing certificates into a Java keystore by hand, the newer release lets the outbound proxy section point at an exported root CA file. Only traffic going back to the StackHawk platform crosses that proxy, while the scanner's traffic to the target application should stay on the same network. The presenters also note that firewalls may need to allow specific StackHawk API hosts.

talks.summary:
This webinar, presented by StackHawk's CSO Scott Gerlock and PagerDuty security engineer James berthodi, examines why application security programs struggle after findings are produced. They argue that finding issues is the easier half, since security teams are often measured on what they find while development teams are measured on shipping. Results that arrive after code is in production interrupt developers, who must reconstruct context before they can fix anything.

The middle of the session treats shift left as an interdependent three-legged stool of people, process and technology, rather than a linear sequence. Practical advice included learning the deployment pipeline firsthand, such as deploying a microservice, and building relationships with engineering teams by listening before offering help. The speakers described a decision framework that separates who recommends, performs, provides input and decides, with development or product leadership usually holding the final call. For tools, they urged testing a proof of concept by actually fixing a vulnerability, and checking whether basic developer workflows, such as cloning a repository and scanning it from the command line, are simple.

The closing points were that tools cannot break silos on their own, that decisions should be documented as a source of truth, and that teams should evolve their approach with feedback rather than aim for a perfect design from the start.

talks.summary:
Legacy dynamic application security testing often lands on production apps with slow scans and findings that reach developers long after the relevant code changed. The session positions StackHawk as DAST meant for every pull request and commit in CI/CD, with configuration aimed at developers rather than a small application security team alone.

The presenter walks through three GitHub integrations: the HawkScan action in GitHub Actions, marketplace pull request checks that post findings and status back to the PR, and CodeQL correlation so static analysis lines up with runtime DAST hits via shared CWE identifiers. A live demo uses a Volnode Express sample repo—stackhawk.yaml with failure threshold, commit and branch tags, and a workflow that builds, runs unit tests, starts the app on the runner, and scans localhost:3000.

After a trivial PR triggers a failed high-severity check, the audience sees bot comments, official status checks, and platform finding details for issues such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. For the prioritized SQL injection case, CodeQL surfaces file and line guidance (service search.js, line six) beside DAST request-response evidence, illustrating how practitioners can close the loop inside GitHub without leaving familiar review workflows.

talks.title: Teams: Secure Your Entire Flock
talks.teaser: Coverage of Teams: Secure Your Entire Flock from the conference program.
talks.summary:
# Overview
This walkthrough introduces StackHawk Teams, a feature designed to help organizations group and organize their applications while ensuring team members follow the principle of least privilege by accessing only the features and applications necessary for their roles.

# Key Topics
- **Role-Based Access Control and the Member Role**: StackHawk previously supported Owner (access to all settings) and Admin (access to all settings except billing). The presentation introduces the "Member" role, which restricts users from organization-level settings such as audit logs, integrations, user management, and team setup, leaving them access only to their personal profiles.
- **API Key Role Restrictions**: API keys generated by individual users automatically inherit and are bound by the permission restrictions of that user's assigned role.
- **Teams Organization and Scoping**: The Teams capability enables administrators to group specific applications together and assign designated users to those teams. Once assigned, users and admins can use a teams dropdown selector to filter views and interact strictly with applications assigned to that team.
- **Application Access Scoping for Members**: Demonstrating from the account of a user named Jordy, members only see and access the specific applications mapped to the team they belong to, preventing unauthorized access across broader organizational assets.
- **Enterprise Availability**: The Teams functionality is provided to customers on the Enterprise plan and is also accessible during trial periods with Enterprise features enabled.

# Technical Details
- **Roles Breakdown**:
  - **Owner**: Complete access to all account settings, including administrative and billing controls.
  - **Admin**: Complete access to all settings except billing.
  - **Member**: Restricted from organization-level controls (audit logs, integrations, user management, team setup); restricted to personal profile management.
- **API Enforcement**: Inherited role permissions apply down to generated API keys.
- **Interface Workflow**: Setup occurs via an admin account to create a team, map specific applications into it, and add users. A teams dropdown filter updates the console UI to isolate the scoped applications.

# Takeaways
StackHawk Teams enables organizations with growing teams to maintain tight access controls over their application security testing workflows. By combining the Member role with team-level application assignments, organizations ensure team members can only test and view the applications required for their specific work. Support is available via in-app chat or at support@stackhawk.com.

After patching the unsanitized query, the presenter uses rescan, which reruns only the plugins that raised alerts in the last scan, to confirm the fix before committing. The session also covered mapping repositories to applications through the GitHub app, scan tags such as commit SHA and branch name for other CI providers, and the failure threshold setting for high, medium or low findings. That threshold makes the scanner exit with an error and fails the commit status. Audience questions covered language independence, since the scanner targets any running HTTP or HTTPS application, and keeping the Docker-packaged scanner current.

The closing segment covered reporting, including per-scan and organization-level reports and an API, audit activity from the triage pane, and running the scanner locally, in Kubernetes or ECS, or from Ansible. talks.title: Custom Test Data for GraphQL APIs
talks.teaser: Shows how to feed custom and Faker-generated values into GraphQL mutation parameters during a HawkScan run.
talks.summary:
StackHawk introduces a feature in HawkScan version 2.9.0 that lets the scanner use user-supplied values, or generated ones, for parameters in a GraphQL schema. It mirrors the custom test data option for REST APIs that was added in the previous release, 2.8.0. The demo runs against a deliberately vulnerable GraphQL application that the team uses to test its scanner.

Setup happens in the StackHawk YAML configuration. A custom variables list names each target field and gives a list of candidate values, and the scanner picks one at random on each run. In the example, the register mutation's first name and last name draw from two custom options each. For the username, the Faker library is switched on with a flag that defaults to false, and a prefixed placeholder requests an email-format value, so a new one is produced every run. After the scan, the spidered GraphQL routes are listed, and a new operations tab on the scan summary shows the queries and mutations registered for that scan. The register mutation's variables display the chosen custom names and the generated email.

The takeaway is that realistic inputs can get past validation and reach more of an application's logic, which may expose more vulnerabilities.

talks.title: GitHub Pull Request Checks with StackHawk
talks.teaser: Shows how StackHawk's GitHub app adds scan status, pull request comments and commit checks to a CI build.
talks.summary:
Brandon from StackHawk presents the new pull request checks feature in the StackHawk GitHub app. The demo uses a service whose StackHawk configuration file and build script run in GitHub Actions, although the speaker notes that other CI/CD providers can be used. A scan tag carries the commit SHA and branch name from the CI build into the StackHawk platform, so each scan can be traced back to where it came from. Because the GitHub app maps the StackHawk application to the repository, results show up inside GitHub.

On a feature branch with a small code change and an open pull request, the build and scan start automatically. A pending Hawk scan commit status appears with a details link to the platform. When the scan finishes, a pull request comment summarizes the findings with a link back to the platform, and the commit status changes to success.

To show failure handling, the speaker commits an intentional configuration error to the StackHawk file. The commit status changes to error, and the comment reports that the scan failed with a brief explanation of why it could not run. The full error details remain reachable from either the comment or the status. The takeaway is that developers can see scan results and scan failures without leaving the pull request.

talks.title: Deeper API Security Test Coverage Webinar
talks.teaser: Demos new DAST features for API testing: custom test data, Postman and Cypress discovery, and custom tenancy checks.
talks.summary:
Presenters from StackHawk argue that application security teams are outnumbered by developers, so security testing has to move earlier and into developers' hands. They make the case for dynamic application security testing (DAST) as a way to find issues that are discoverable and exploitable in a running HTTP application, including REST, SOAP and GraphQL APIs. They explain why API scans are often slow: scanners that drive a browser can crawl the same records over and over, and valid input values are needed to reach deeper into an API.

The middle of the session covers recent releases. Custom test data lets teams supply specific values, invalid inputs and faker-generated data such as well-formed email addresses. Custom scan discovery accepts existing Postman collections and Cypress specs, and custom test scripts can check business logic such as tenancy. In a live demo against a sample pants-retailer API, a scan flagged a SQL injection that the presenter reproduced with a replayed request, plus a custom tenant-filtering alert. A connected static analysis tool pointed to the line where the query ran.

Triage comes last. Marking findings as false positives or risk accepted is remembered across scans, so later runs surface mainly new issues. Jira and DefectDojo are supported for tickets, with webhooks and API access for other systems, and Azure DevOps was described as planned. The takeaway is to keep the test configuration in the repository so every developer runs the same checks while building code.

talks.title: Deeper API Security Test Coverage Office Hours
talks.teaser: Demonstrates custom scan discovery, custom test data and custom test scripts for extending StackHawk API security scans.
talks.summary:
This casual office hours session followed StackHawk's launch of deeper API security testing. Engineering leads and solutions architects demonstrated three new features and then took live and pre-submitted questions. The core problem raised is that scanners often filled REST API parameters with static values, which seldom reached deeper application logic.

Sam Bolin showed custom scan discovery, where an existing Cypress end-to-end test run is added to the scan configuration. The browser test traffic lets the scanner find paths it would otherwise miss, including a hidden test path. Austin Parrigan covered custom test data, which lets teams supply their own values, such as test user IDs, or generate formatted values with the Faker library, such as email-formatted usernames. He noted that password reset flows are a good case, because valid test IDs get past an early 404 and reach the logic behind it. Dana White demonstrated custom test scripts migrated from ZAP active scripts, using a JWT none-algorithm check. She showed how a script is registered as a plugin with an ID and run under a custom scripts policy.

In the Q&A, a solutions architect explained that DAST tools run automatically in CI/CD, so new vulnerabilities are caught as code changes, while penetration tests usually happen later and less often. The team said policy management, which will control which plugins and tests run, was coming soon, along with CLI support for listing and removing script plugin IDs. The main takeaway is that teams can reuse existing end-to-end test tooling and add business-specific checks to exercise more of their APIs before release.

talks.title: Custom Scan Discovery Overview
talks.teaser: Custom scan discovery wires developer and QA CLI tools into HawkScan so routes are found before authenticated active testing begins.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces custom scan discovery in HawkScan, StackHawk’s dynamic application security testing scanner for server-rendered apps, REST, GraphQL, and similar targets. Instead of relying only on built-in crawling, teams supply a shell command that generates HTTP traffic; HawkScan runs that command in the caller’s environment, sets proxy variables so the traffic flows through the scanner, and reads configuration from the StackHawk YAML file with optional environment-variable interpolation for secrets and runtime options.

A walkthrough uses curl pointed at a local app so HawkScan records a route and reuses it during the active scan phase, giving security teams precise control over which paths enter testing. A second example swaps curl for Newman against a Postman collection with URLs, query parameters, and variables. Newman runs without auth and hits 401 or 403 responses, yet HawkScan still learns the paths; separate HawkScan username, password, and cookie settings then drive authenticated testing on those routes.

The speaker notes that scripted authentication is straightforward for well-built apps and that running custom discovery against localhost over HTTP tends to work more smoothly than remote HTTPS targets. Any CLI that emits HTTP traffic can feed the scanner, letting teams reuse existing QA and development workflows. Documentation on docs.stackhawk.com covers deeper configuration; the closing emphasis is finding bugs earlier in development to improve application security posture.

talks.title: Custom Test Scripts Overview
talks.teaser: A short walkthrough shows how to register JavaScript custom test plugins in StackHawk and raise alerts when scans expose cross-tenant data.
talks.summary:
The session introduces custom test scripts for StackHawk as a way to ship organization-specific scan rules alongside built-in checks. A script is registered with the platform to obtain a unique plugin identifier, then wired into StackHawk YAML with a fully qualified name, script type, path, and language. Scripts live under type-specific directories so the scanner can discover them.

The demo uses a tenancy-check plugin implemented in JavaScript with the scanNode hook, which runs once per node. The code copies the active HTTP message, appends a path segment intended to reveal users, and compares a known user identifier from another company against the logged-in tenant context in a Java Spring deployment. When the wrong user appears, the script records evidence in the response body and raises an alert with the plugin ID, message, and index; risk, title, description, and solution fields are left to the author.

After starting a Hawk scan, the custom finding appears like any other result, tagged to show it came from the custom script and ready for triage. Practitioners should treat custom scripts as first-class plugins: register IDs correctly, keep YAML valid, implement scan or scanNode as needed, and encode clear alert metadata for downstream diagnosis.

talks.title: Helping Developers Go Faster, Safer
talks.teaser: Links application security to trust, churn, and deal friction, then argues for shift-left testing that developers can run locally and in CI.
talks.summary:
The session opens by challenging common but vague rationales for application security and urging leaders to tie programs to outcomes the business already measures: customer trust, acquisition cost, time to close deals, churn, and selective regulatory obligations. It contrasts breach horror stories with metrics engineering and product leaders can actually model with finance and sales.

A motorsport analogy frames security as enabling speed rather than erecting production speed bumps. The middle covers why infrequent, production-only security testing fails at modern delivery scale, the cost curve of fixing defects late versus in development, and the difference between empowering developers (“shift left”) versus dumping tools on them (“chuck left”). Practical guidance favors SCA, static analysis, and dynamic testing with correlated findings, local reproduction of failures, CI parity, triage agreements, and cross-functional buy-in before purchasing tools.

The close recaps treating application security as a delivery problem: instrument lightweight checks early, let engineers own fixes with security consulting on hard issues, tune and document false positives, and prioritize new findings over legacy backlogs while relating severe items to revenue and retention metrics. Q&A reinforces conversations with product and engineering leadership and operational habits like not blocking developers on unreproducible CI-only scans.

talks.title: and Snyk Integration Webinar
talks.teaser: Demonstrates correlating DAST and SAST findings from StackHawk and Snyk Code to help developers prioritize and fix flaws.
talks.summary:
This StackHawk and Snyk webinar addresses how application security testing can move into the developer workflow. The speakers argue that security bugs get more expensive to fix the later they are found, and that legacy dynamic testing tends to be slow, hard to set up and run only periodically. They frame dynamic testing (DAST) as exercising a running application from the outside, while static testing (SAST) reads source code, and explain how the two complement each other.

The demo uses a sample API with planted flaws. A StackHawk scan, configured in a YAML file and fed an OpenAPI spec, reports a SQL injection and a cross-site scripting issue against a pre-production build. The matching Snyk Code results point to the same vulnerable search service inside the IDE. The integration correlates findings by CWE identifier, which the speakers describe as a first version that should improve with feedback. The presenter then fixes the query by switching to parameterized queries and reruns both tools to confirm the SQL injection is gone.

The closing part covers practical points: the scanner can run on a laptop, in CI/CD or in a private cloud, and a failure threshold can return a non-zero exit code to gate builds on untriaged high-severity findings. The speakers note that the Snyk side needs API access enabled through support and that the StackHawk side requires an enterprise plan for this feature. The main takeaway is to test early and often, and to use matched results to decide what to fix first.

talks.title: Snyk + StackHawk Webinar: Moving Towards Continuous Application Security
talks.teaser: Engineering leaders explore shifting appsec left with DevOps-paced pipelines, champion programs, and developer-first security tooling.
talks.summary:
The session opens on a familiar tension: security reviews and staging gates cannot keep pace when teams ship to production many times a day or week. The framing treats engineering as a race program—application code as the car, infrastructure as the track, and security as the safety function that must stay involved without stalling delivery.

Scott Gerlach walks through how static analysis, dynamic analysis, and software composition checking mirror linting, integration testing, and incoming parts inspection. He contrasts passive “deploy and hope” choices with active tradeoffs, argues pen testing and bug bounty work best after automated scans remove easy issues, and advises embedding a collaborative appsec hire inside engineering rather than a distant gatekeeping team. Simon Maple builds on dev ownership at scale when ratios near one security person per hundred developers, emphasizing scorecards, top-down accountability, security champions, shared goals, and making the secure path the easy path through automation in IDEs, pull requests, and CI.

Both speakers stress starting with visibility before blocking builds, ratcheting policy as teams build muscle, correlating SCA, SAST, and DAST signals to prioritize fixes, and treating APIs and infrastructure-as-code as first-class appsec surfaces. A moderated Q&A covers first security hires versus a CISO, when to run tools locally versus in CI, minimum secure-coding literacy for developers, and decoupled API testing for microservice teams.

talks.title: Introducing the StackHawk CLI: Technical Demo
talks.teaser: Shows how to install, authenticate and validate the StackHawk CLI, then run scans against a vulnerable Java Spring app.
talks.summary:
The presenter introduces the StackHawk CLI, a command-line tool for finding and fixing application security bugs. Earlier scans needed Docker images containing the scanner, but the CLI runs scans without Docker and offers a small set of commands for starting scans and checking configuration files.

The walkthrough covers installing the tool through Homebrew or a downloaded zip file, then confirming a 2.0 beta version. Authentication with hawk init uses an API key issued when a user account is created, and the presenter registers a web application on the platform with its host URL and an OpenAPI REST API type. The help output lists init, version, scan and validate subcommands, along with flags to override the API key and disable colored output. Validation is shown three ways: a default stackhawk.yaml file found automatically, a file with three configuration problems reported inline, and a file that fails YAML parsing entirely.

With a valid configuration, a scan runs against a Java Spring application with known vulnerabilities, and findings appear in the terminal and on the platform, where each one can be opened for detail. The closing section demonstrates scan flags for passing the API key, app ID and app host, enabling debug logging, and setting the repository directory and configuration file explicitly.

talks.title: ZAP DeepDive: ZAP 2.11.0
talks.teaser: Coverage of ZAP DeepDive: ZAP 2.11.0 from the conference program.
talks.summary:
Simon Bennetts walks StackHawk engineers through OWASP ZAP 2.11.0, stressing that the desktop UI looks familiar while automation and reporting engines matured underneath. New alert tags attach OWASP Top 10 2017 and 2021 labels (plus custom key-value tags editable in the UI or API) so CI pipelines can slice findings by compliance framework.

The bundled Automation Framework replaces ad hoc command-line and Docker package-scan scripts with one YAML plan: contexts, spider jobs, passive waits, active attacks, sanity tests, and report steps runnable from the GUI or headless CLI. Reporting moved to Thymeleaf templates with richer HTML exports, optional request and response bodies, and docker images that will refresh monthly even between core releases.

Alpha add-ons cover out-of-band interaction services and per-alert retesting, while an expanded statistics API feeds automation assertions on spider counts and auth state. Bennetts points readers to blog posts and future deep dives rather than demoing every toggle.

talks.title: JS Security Testing in GitHub Actions Workshop | Vue.js 2021
talks.teaser: Hands-on steps wire dependency scanning, static analysis, and dynamic testing into GitHub Actions for a vulnerable Node Express app.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing three common automated security test classes—software composition analysis on dependency manifests, static analysis over source patterns, and dynamic probing of a running HTTP service—and explains when each fits web APIs versus other application shapes. Participants fork a deliberately weak Node Express sample, then build a GitHub Actions workflow that checks out code, installs Node 14, and runs a clean npm install, fixing typical YAML indentation and marketplace action naming pitfalls along the way.

The middle segment enables Dependabot dependency graph features, reviews severity-labeled alerts tied to CVE advisories, and merges an auto-generated upgrade pull request that reuses the new pipeline. CodeQL code scanning is added via another workflow, including scheduled runs and a demonstrated high-severity finding: a SQL query assembled from unvalidated user input in a search route. The closing portion registers a StackHawk account, stores an API key in GitHub secrets, adds stackhawk.yaml targeting localhost port 3000, and extends the pipeline to start the app in the background before HawkScan runs in Docker.

Scan results surface cross-site scripting, SQL injection, and related issues with replayable request and response evidence, triage options, and optional pipeline failure on unresolved highs. Takeaways include starting with effortless composition scanning, prioritizing dynamic scans for web surfaces, keeping secrets out of repositories, and treating aggressive DAST as inappropriate for production without safeguards.

talks.title: ZAP DeepDive: WebSockets
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how OWASP ZAP captures, filters, fuzzes, and scripts WebSocket traffic for manual and automated security testing.
talks.summary:
WebSockets give browsers and servers full-duplex messaging without the rigid request-response shape of classic HTTP, but payloads are often opaque text—JSON, XML, CSV, or custom formats—so security tools must treat each channel on its own terms. The session positions ZAP as an early and still strong option for WebSocket testing and walks through live use against a public echo site.

In the UI, testers open dedicated WebSocket tabs to list channels, read handshakes from the HTTP upgrade, filter by opcode or payload, resend messages, and set global or payload-specific breakpoints to edit traffic mid-flight—mirroring familiar HTTP proxy workflows. The demo extends to fuzzing selected message fragments with file-based attack lists, tuning add-on options such as forwarding all socket traffic, breaking on pings, and stripping Sec-WebSocket-Extensions for stable interception, plus JavaScript and Groovy scripts for processors, per-message senders, and passive checks that flag patterns like card numbers, email addresses, and application errors.

Practitioners also get a brief map of the REST API for listing channels, sending text, and managing breaks, and pointers to the websocket add-on source and community script contributions. Secure WebSocket (WSS) needs no separate proxy setup beyond ordinary ZAP use.

talks.title: ZAP DeepDive: Zest Scripting Part 3
talks.teaser: Demonstrates Zest client-side browser scripts in ZAP for authenticated scans, persona workflows, and statement options.
talks.summary:
Client-side Zest scripting extends OWASP ZAP when manipulating and replaying HTTP traffic alone cannot complete a test. The session is the third installment on Zest, aimed at flows that need a real browser—clicks, typing, frames, and multiple windows—rather than server-side request edits alone.

Against OWASP Juice Shop, the presenter builds standalone client scripts step by step: launching Firefox, opening the login route to avoid a welcome overlay, and walking through Google SSO until an interstitial blocks automation. He then parameterizes local login, invokes an existing server-side Zest register script to create the account, and finishes sign-in in the browser. A longer Persona-era example registers random accounts, tracks a new window, polls Mailinator for confirmation mail, and loops so each run could use a fresh username when testing input restrictions. He stresses that client scripts break easily when providers or DOMs change, and closes with a tour of Zest statement types—launch, element interaction, conditionals, loops, scan hooks, and script calls—plus where Zest and ZAP add-on code live.

Takeaways for practitioners: add one client statement at a time, prefer stable locators such as element IDs, combine client and server Zest where registration fits the wire but login needs the UI, and treat browser automation as maintenance-heavy compared to pure request replay.

talks.title: ZAPCon 2021 After Hours: Adding ZAP to All Your Testing
talks.teaser: ZAPCon 2021 After Hours: Adding ZAP to All Your Testing.
talks.summary:
HMRC Multi Channel Digital Tax Platform leaders Marcus Swann and Simon Granger describe how they normalized OWASP ZAP across hundreds of microservices without trading delivery speed for security after COVID-era emergency releases. They pair AppSec 101 curriculum rollout with a three-part platform kit: an automated Docker sidecar builder, a Python control client that starts ZAP gently and archives reports, and Jenkins Job Builder templates that inject ZAP into existing Groovy pipelines instead of the deprecated official plug-in.

The sidecar layers HMRC-selected ZAP add-ons atop `zap2docker-stable`, loops post-scan scripts to harvest artifacts, and exposes knobs for proxied URL coverage, scanner toggles, alert filters, and fail-on severity thresholds. Q&A invites teams to workshop adoption and to watch Bennetts’s emerging YAML automation framework as a future migration path.

talks.title: ZAP DeepDive: Zest Scripting Part 2
talks.teaser: Builds on Zest in OWASP ZAP with targeted scripts, scan rules, and cross-script globals for practical testing workflows.
talks.summary:
The session continues hands-on Zest training after an earlier introduction to standalone scripts, loops, and pulling values from responses for later requests. The presenter walks through a shipped targeted script that turns POST requests into GET by moving the body onto the URL, then builds a new targeted script that does the reverse for GET or PUT traffic by stripping query parameters into the POST body. A caching quirk forces a ZAP restart before the live demo succeeds.

Zest fits request manipulation better than low-level script types such as encode-decode input vectors. The walkthrough adds a passive scan rule that flags responses matching an HTTP status pattern and “internal server error,” then an active scan rule that appends a debug parameter and raises an alert when the response body suggests SQL output. Both illustrate quick, GUI-driven checks without wrestling with full scripting syntax.

Global variables close the loop: Graal JS and Zest scripts can set and read the same globals, enabling data exchange across script languages. The talk previews a third installment focused on client-side Zest capabilities.

talks.title: ZAPCon 2021 After Hours: Security Automation with ZAP
talks.teaser: Shows how to automate web application security scans with ZAP, including scans behind a login.
talks.summary:
This after-hours session from ZAPCon 2021 focuses on security automation with the ZAP web application scanner. It opens by framing application security and why scanning is worth automating rather than running by hand.

The middle of the talk moves into practical setup. The speaker describes pointing automated scans at web applications that sit behind a login page, supplying a username and password so the scanner can reach authenticated areas. Scheduling scans to run at set times, so they recur without manual effort, is also covered, along with the problems and challenges that come up when scans run unattended.

The closing portion wraps up the session and thanks the audience. For practitioners, the main takeaway is that ZAP can be built into a routine workflow so application checks run repeatedly, and that authenticated scanning needs particular care to reach the parts of an application that matter most.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Zest Scripting Part 1
talks.teaser: Coverage of ZAP Deep Dive: Zest Scripting Part 1 from the conference program.
talks.summary:
Simon Bennetts introduces Mozilla-originated Zest as a JSON macro language for security tools, now maintained under OWASP ZAP. He builds a hello-world standalone script, runs it from Gradle on the CLI, then records Budget Store traffic into a script with default status and length assertions that prove replays succeeded.

Juice Shop registration flows show swapping hard-coded emails for random assignments, extracting user IDs between requests, and tightening assertions to match success text. Parameters, nested script calls, for-loop batching, and LDAP fuzz payloads demonstrate how GUI-recorded steps become CI-friendly repro scripts without hand-writing JSON.
