talks.title: Scanning REST APIs
talks.teaser: Shows how to configure StackHawk to scan REST APIs using an OpenAPI spec and token-based authentication.
talks.summary:
This short video explains how to set up StackHawk, a dynamic application security testing tool, so it can scan a REST API. The configuration needs an application ID, an environment name, and the host where the API runs during the scan. Enabling auto policy lets the scanner send only the tests that are relevant to the API.

The presenter then shows how the OpenAPI specification is referenced, either as a local file relative to the project or as a route on the host. Giving the scanner the spec seeds it with the API's routes, so it does not have to discover endpoints on its own and can send better-matched tests to each one. The authentication section covers a logged-in indicator, such as a regex or a query matching a 200 status, and a logged-out indicator tied to a 401. It then walks through a JSON form login that posts username and password fields to a login path. A token is extracted from the response body under a named field and returned on later requests as a Bearer credential in the Authorization header.

Finally, a test path is defined so the credentials can be validated before the scan starts. That check helps avoid a log full of 400-level responses caused by failed authentication. The takeaway is that a handful of configuration entries covering the host, the spec, the authentication state, and token handling is all that is needed to scan a REST API.

talks.title: ZAPCon 2021 After Hours: Starting a Security Program on a Shoestring (with ZAP)
talks.teaser: Explains how small web teams can seed a security program by running OWASP ZAP, validating alerts, and turning fixes into written practice.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a familiar constraint: a small development group ships a web application, has little money, and suddenly needs credible security progress without hiring a full program upfront. Rather than attempting threat modeling, training, and enterprise tooling all at once, it argues for starting with dynamic application security testing and learning directly from what the scanner surfaces.

It contrasts network, static, composition, and dynamic scanners, then walks through practical selection criteria—free software, active maintenance, broad detection, readable reports, and eventual build integration—landing on OWASP ZAP as a sustained choice. Using the deliberately vulnerable Mutillidae site, it decodes typical ZAP alert fields and demonstrates reproducing a high-severity path traversal and a SQL injection on a login form, including why boolean-based checks can differ across paired requests. It also warns that findings may be false positives or overweighted without site context.

The closing arc treats a prioritized backlog as a curriculum: fix issues, reuse defenses like input validation and safer errors, commit to scan cadence in a team working agreement, add secure coding notes and onboarding checks, and review trends over time. That path yields audit-friendly artifacts and nudges the organization toward vulnerability management and a fuller secure development lifecycle while acknowledging scanners alone cannot guarantee completeness.

talks.title: ZAPCon 2021: ZAP Project Updates
talks.teaser: Coverage of ZAPCon 2021: ZAP Project Updates from the conference program.
talks.summary:
At ZAPCon 2021 Simon Bennetts explains why ZAP needed a fresh automation framework despite existing command-line, Docker package scan, and raw API options. The new add-on-driven design runs entirely inside ZAP with one YAML file describing contexts, add-on management, passive and active scan jobs, and sanity checks that can fail builds when too few URLs appear.

Live demos run minimal and tuned configs against a local Juice Shop target, turning off most active rules to surface a single reflected XSS finding faster than legacy package scans. He previews forthcoming authentication support, ajax spider integration, and OpenAPI, SOAP, and GraphQL add-ons while urging early adopters to file gaps before production rollouts.

A companion reporting add-on rebuilds exports on Thymeleaf with customizable HTML, planned PDF and JSON outputs, and a paid template competition stressing accessibility. Q&A covers headless `-cmd` usage, docker weekly images, false-positive workflows, and upcoming deep-dive videos.

talks.title: ZAPCon 2021: Mobile Application Security Testing with ZAP
talks.teaser: Shows how to proxy iOS and Android app traffic through OWASP ZAP, run scans, and catch issues such as broken authorization.
talks.summary:
The session walks through end-to-end mobile application security testing using OWASP ZAP as a man-in-the-middle proxy. Presenters outline prerequisites: a ZAP-capable workstation, a phone or emulator on the same Wi‑Fi, and installing ZAP’s dynamic root CA so TLS traffic can be decrypted. For iOS they transfer the certificate via a small Python 2 HTTP server on port 8888, configure manual Wi‑Fi proxy to the lab IP on 8080, install the profile, and enable full trust for the ZAP root. For Android they copy the cert directly, install it for Wi‑Fi and VPN/apps on older builds, clear conflicting credentials, accept the monitoring warning, and point Wi‑Fi proxy settings at the ZAP host on 8080. Recorded demos show intercepting HTTPS to apple.com and demo.testfire.net.

They compare physical devices with emulators, favoring real hardware for fidelity (haptics, app conflicts, banking apps that block simulators) while noting emulators are cheaper and easier for some memory-focused work. Traffic analysis is framed against OWASP Mobile Top 10 themes such as insecure communication and authorization. An automated scan against OWASP GoatDroid with login context is shown, followed by a manual privilege-escalation case: intercepting a logged-in “general” user’s traffic and toggling an admin flag in the request to unlock manage-user functionality.

Q&A covers SSL pinning bypass options (Frida with root or emulator versus low-success APK/IPA cert swaps), that Wi‑Fi proxy routing sends device traffic destined for the configured proxy port through ZAP rather than every protocol blindly, malware C2 visibility via the same pattern, and corporate firewall or endpoint hurdles when binding ZAP to all interfaces.

talks.title: ZAPCon 2021: ZAP in Pakistani Fintech
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn how a Pakistani payment vendor wired OWASP ZAP into TFS builds with Gauge and parameterized scans.
talks.summary:
Salman Khawaja and Hamad Hassan describe application security work at TPS Pakistan, a payment vendor whose software reaches a large share of domestic banks and international clients. They argue that repeating manual tests across similar deployments wastes effort, and that automating dynamic scans is essential when the same product ships to many environments.

Their stack combines Gauge with Python, OWASP ZAP, and on-prem TFS build agents. Pipeline parameters supply target and login URLs, credentials, CSRF data, a login-success indicator, and toggles for spidering, Ajax spidering, passive scan, and active scan. A demo queues a build that runs PowerShell on an agent, drives ZAP through login, executes a short passive scan, and attaches HTML reports to the build. They chose ZAP over commercial scanners mainly for API-level control and maintainability; framework setup took roughly two to three months, with about three to four weeks to wire each new product.

They plan API coverage, session reuse, richer spider controls, and tighter scan policies. In Q&A they estimate automated ZAP covers on the order of 60 to 70 percent of routine assurance when no high findings appear, with business logic and deeper issues still needing manual testing. Deployment teams can trigger scans weekly without writing code, using only the parameterized build form.

talks.title: ZAPCon 2021: Enhacing ZAP with Feedback Based Fuzzing
talks.teaser: Shows how coverage-guided Jazzer fuzzing can feed requests to ZAP's active scanner to test web applications more effectively.
talks.summary:
Fuzzing usually throws random data at a program, which rarely gets past early input checks or reaches deep code. This talk explains how coverage-guided fuzzing addresses that by instrumenting the target, so the fuzzer can see which code paths each input touches and which constants it is compared against. The presenter illustrates this with an image parser that the fuzzer eventually fed valid images without knowing the format. He then introduces Jazzer, a coverage-guided fuzzer for JVM code built on libFuzzer, and demonstrates a small harness that found a cross-site scripting issue in a JSON sanitizer library, running at more than 53 thousand executions per second on one laptop core.

The middle of the talk turns to web applications, where requests must follow a structure, so random bytes are rejected early. Jazzer's web mutator works from an API definition so generated requests stay valid. Requests that reach new coverage are forwarded to ZAP, whose active scanners then attack them, so ZAP spends its effort on distinct code paths rather than near-identical requests. A corpus of interesting inputs is saved between runs, which lets later scans resume and re-test past crashes. In a deliberately vulnerable Spring application, string comparison feedback let the fuzzer guess a username needed to reach a SQL injection.

The presenter concludes that the combined setup gave better results than either tool alone. He suggests the community work toward standard interfaces so dynamic analysis tools can share results, and mentions plans to release instrumentation-based bug detectors for JVM applications.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Setting Up a ZAP Dev Environment
talks.teaser: ZAP Deep Dive: Setting Up a ZAP Dev Environment.
talks.summary:
Simon Bennetts live-builds OWASP ZAP from source for StackHawk engineers, cloning `zaproxy` and running `./gradlew run` to show how core-only checkouts miss marketplace add-ons until `zap-extensions` is copied beside the main repo and weekly add-ons are synchronized.

He imports both Gradle projects into Eclipse, fixes the working directory to `zap/src/main/dist`, deploys the Simple Example add-on, edits `Message.properties`, and hot-reloads via `gradlew :addOns:simpleExample:deployZapAddOnOnZap` against a non-default API port. A follow-on exercise copies Simple Example into a new Deep Dive add-on, updates Gradle settings, and proves renamed UI strings appear after deploy.

Bennetts ends with breakpoint debugging of extension constructors by attaching Simple Example sources in the run configuration, encouraging contributors to fork add-ons rather than patch core when experimenting.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Report Generation
talks.teaser: Shows how ZAP's reporting add-on enables filtered exports and customizable Thymeleaf templates across several output formats.
talks.summary:
Legacy ZAP reporting offered little beyond picking HTML, XML, Markdown, or JSON and saving a file. Outputs had changed little in roughly a decade, leaned on XSLT, and mainly summarized alerts with limited scope. The talk positions a new marketplace add-on released around ZAPCon as a replaceable, more flexible framework.

The walkthrough covers installing the official Reports add-on, using the Generate Report dialog, and scoping contexts and sites. It demonstrates risk and confidence filters, optional inclusion of request and response data, and outputs in HTML, XML, Markdown, and PDF. Template layout lives under the ZAP reports directory with template.yaml metadata and Thymeleaf-driven report files; naming patterns support site placeholders and date formatting. PDF generation reuses HTML templates but requires well-formed markup. Built-in help and user-guide material document fields, the alerts tree passed into templates, lazy reads from the message database, and planned automation-framework integration. Source for the extension sits in the ZAP add-ons tree, and a template competition offers cash rewards for contributed HTML and PDF designs with accessibility expectations.

Planned work includes embedded resources, richer data plugins, API support, per-template custom fields, and selectable report sections such as charts. A closing question clarifies that under the automation framework, failed jobs can skip report generation unless warnings are configured to continue anyway.

talks.title: Adding Application Security Testing to Your GitLab Pipeline
talks.teaser: Shows how dynamic application security testing can run inside a GitLab pipeline and block builds on untriaged high findings.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the cost of security bugs, which grows the later in the lifecycle they are found. The speaker argues that security tests are hard to write by hand because they check what should not happen, so tools built for developers help teams catch issues while they code. He compares static analysis of source code and dependencies with dynamic testing, which probes a running application from the outside as an attacker would and, in his view, produces fewer false positives.

The demo used a deliberately vulnerable Django polls app started with Docker Compose inside a GitLab CI job. The scanner crawled the running app and reported a reflected cross-site scripting issue on the search path. The speaker traced it to auto-escaping being turned off in a template, restored escaping, and pushed the change so the pipeline reran. He also covered triage options such as risk accepted and false positive, a failure threshold that fails the build on untriaged highs, and triage history that the scanner keeps between runs. A SQL injection finding surfaced later in the scan, and a known scanner bug caused one run to fail.

The takeaway is to add dynamic testing alongside software composition analysis, return results to the developers who can fix them, and gate builds only on issues teams can act on. Security staff can then help prioritise fixes instead of handing over long ticket lists. The product described is a software-as-a-service platform priced per user, with a free tier for one application.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Authenticated Packaged Scans
talks.teaser: ZAP Deep Dive: Authenticated Packaged Scans.
talks.summary:
Simon Bennetts demonstrates authenticated scanning with ZAP’s Docker baseline package against his local BodgeIt store app. He first proves a container cannot reach `localhost` on the host, replaces it with the machine’s LAN IP, and validates an unauthenticated baseline before layering login.

In the desktop UI he creates a budget context, flags the POST login request, sets cookie session management, defines logged-in and logged-out regex indicators, and enables forced user mode to prove ZAP can silently re-authenticate. Authentication statistics via the API show mostly logged-in spider traffic once indicators are tuned.

For automation he exports the context XML, bind-mounts it into `zap2docker-stable`, passes `-c` and user flags, adds a Python `pre_shutdown` hook that queries `stats.auth` through the API, and warns that file parameters require `-v $(pwd):/zap/wrk`. The pattern mirrors full scans and works headless with WebSwing when a desktop UI is unavailable.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: ZAP Automation
talks.teaser: Coverage of ZAP Deep Dive: ZAP Automation from the conference program.
talks.summary:
Simon Bennetts walks StackHawk engineers through every mature path to automate OWASP ZAP, starting with quick `-cmd`/`quickurl` runs that exit when finished, then warning that bare command-line mode is too rigid for serious CI. He contrasts unsupported Jenkins plug-ins with the recommended Docker package scans: baseline passive-only spidering, full active attacks, and OpenAPI, SOAP, or GraphQL importers with hookable Python extension points.

Baseline configuration can emit pass/warn summaries, respect progress files for outstanding fixes, and ignore scoped URLs via generated config files. GitHub Marketplace actions wrap the same images with optional tokens that open and update a single repository issue as findings fluctuate. Bennetts notes all package scans ultimately start ZAP in daemon mode and drive the API, and previews a YAML automation framework add-on meant to supersede the Docker-only scripts.

He closes on operational tips: verify localhost targets are reachable inside the container, prefer desktop reconnaissance before unattended full scans, and use weekly versus live images when chasing bleeding-edge fixes.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Configuration
talks.teaser: Coverage of ZAP Deep Dive: Configuration from the conference program.
talks.summary:
Simon Bennetts tours where ZAP stores per-user settings on macOS, Linux, and Windows, emphasizing `config.xml` for global options and separate directories for contexts, scan policies, scripts, plugins, and logs. He maps GUI toggles to dotted configuration keys used by `-config` and `-configfile` CLI flags, warning that typos silently write unused values.

Contexts export to XML for authentication and scope; policies and editable scripts also live on disk so Docker automation must mount the right folders. He points engineers to `*Param` Java classes when hunting key names and notes log4j2 controls for support escalations.

talks.title: Automating Application Security Testing in CI/CD with StackHawk and Spinnaker
talks.teaser: Shows how a DAST scan runs inside a Spinnaker pipeline that deploys a sample app to Kubernetes.
talks.summary:
This webinar shows how to add dynamic application security testing to a continuous delivery pipeline so that vulnerabilities surface before release. The speakers explain that DAST probes a running application without needing its source code, so it reports only issues that are actually exposed, which tends to mean fewer false positives. StackHawk's scanner reads a short YAML file holding an application ID, an environment and a host, stored in the repository next to the code.

The demo uses a rock paper scissors web app deployed by a pipeline built on Armory's distribution of Spinnaker. A GitHub pull request builds a container image that triggers the pipeline, which deploys to a Kubernetes development environment and then runs the scanner as a job. In the StackHawk dashboard, a high-severity missing anti-CSRF token finding was sent to Jira and fixed by removing an unused jQuery library in a merged pull request. A rescan confirmed the issue was gone. A server version leak at the ingress controller was reproduced manually with curl.

The session closes with Slack, Datadog and Jira integrations and a free developer tier. The scanner suits REST APIs and traditional web apps, and it supports token, cookie, session and form-based authentication. The presenters say a Spinnaker proof of concept can be running in under half an hour, though learning the tool takes days. The takeaway is that pipeline scanning gives developers findings early, with results tracked from scan to scan.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Introduction to ZAP
talks.teaser: Shows how to get the free ZAP web scanner running, from the desktop UI and command line to automated scans.
talks.summary:
Simon Bennetts, the ZAP founder and project lead, opens the first in a series of training sessions on the free, open-source edition of ZAP. He explains that ZAP is a dynamic application security testing tool, so it probes a running application rather than reading its source code the way static analyzers do. He argues that ZAP is well suited to finding new flaws in custom applications, since scanners that only match known software versions tend to miss them. He also stresses that ZAP actively attacks its targets, so only systems you have permission to test should be scanned.

Bennetts then walks through the download options on the project website, covering Windows, Linux and macOS installers and cross-platform packages that need Java 8 or later, plus Docker images and package managers. He runs ZAP from a terminal, pointing it at a clean configuration directory so earlier settings do not interfere, and shows the help output. Launching with no arguments opens the desktop interface, while daemon mode runs ZAP headless on localhost port 8080. He finishes with a quick scan from the command line that runs the spider and then an active scan, writing the findings out as XML, and recommends the API for serious automation.

The last part is a tour of the website's resources, including the getting started guide, desktop user guide, API documentation, descriptions of the built-in alerts, Docker guides, a frequently asked questions page, the bug bounty and contribution guidance. Bennetts closes by previewing the next session on the desktop, which he recommends even for automation because it helps diagnose problems and export configurations for use through the API.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: The ZAP 2.9.0 Desktop Interface
talks.teaser: ZAP Deep Dive: The ZAP 2.9.0 Desktop Interface.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this StackHawk training session, OWASP ZAP founder and project lead Simon Bennetts provides a detailed walkthrough of the OWASP ZAP 2.9.0 desktop interface. Bennetts explains that even for automated pipelines or headless daemon setups, understanding the desktop interface is critical because the UI directly reflects ZAP's underlying data structures, configurations, and API behavior. The session covers core interface navigation, layout customizations, scanning modes, scope definitions, contexts, and technology detection mechanisms.

### Key Topics
- **Session Persistence**: When launching ZAP, users are prompted whether to persist the session. ZAP relies on an underlying HSQLDB database; persisting at startup writes continuously to this database without needing an expensive copy operation upon exit.
- **Interface Layout and Customization**: ZAP features three primary windows: the Sites tree on the left (hierarchical data), a central work area (requests, responses, and settings), and lower information tabs (alerts, spider progress, active scan, history). Layouts can be adjusted, tabs can be revealed via a green tab selector or pinned, and tab names can be hidden for compact displays.
- **Quick Start and Automated Scanning**: The Quick Start tab provides resources (PDF Getting Started guide, desktop user guide, user group) and a streamlined automated scan. Entering a target URL sequentially launches exploration (traditional spider, and optionally AJAX spider) followed by the active scanner.
- **Modes and Contexts**: ZAP offers operational modes including Safe mode (blocks any attacking actions), Protected mode (only allows attacking assets explicitly marked in scope), and Standard mode (allows attacking any target). Contexts group URLs using regexes and serve as the baseline for configuring authentication, custom application structures, and specific technology stacks.
- **Add-on Marketplace & Table Views**: Users can extend ZAP via the add-on marketplace, download released/beta scan rules, and customize information tables using the corner menu on column headers.

### Technical Details
- **Sites Tree Internals**: The Sites tree represents ZAP's internal functional model of the target. ZAP distinguishes between HTTP methods (e.g., GET vs. POST on `/basket`) and path variations, but groups requests with differing parameter values under a single node by default (e.g., searches with different queries are treated as identical functionality).
- **Scan Rules & Technology Filtering**: In active scan policies, rules are assigned based on target technology (such as specific SQL injection rules targeting Oracle, MySQL, MS SQL, or SQLite). When technology filters are applied in a context during white-box testing, scan rules still trigger from the policy but internally check the flag and abort execution if the technology is disabled. Bennetts also demonstrates the Wappalyzer add-on, which operates via the passive scanner to dynamically detect technologies from traffic.

### Takeaways
Familiarity with ZAP's desktop UI accelerates effective automation and API scripting. Correctly configuring contexts, scopes, and technology flags prevents unintended scans and speeds up testing routines. Testing should only be conducted against targets where explicit permission has been granted.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Exploring with the Standard Spider
talks.teaser: Shows how ZAP's traditional spider crawls a web application, which options tune it, and how to drive it through the API.
talks.summary:
ZAP project lead Simon Bennetts opens by explaining why ZAP separates exploring an application from attacking it. Manual exploration through a proxied browser is usually the most effective approach, but it cannot be automated. Unit tests driven through ZAP offer a repeatable alternative. API-only services need imported definitions rather than a crawler.

The main part covers the traditional spider, a standard web crawler that follows HTTP requests and responses to discover new URLs. It is fast but struggles with heavily JavaScript-driven applications, which is why a separate AJAX spider exists. Scans can be started from the automated scan dialog, the spider tab or a right-click on a site node, and contexts and the recurse option control scope. The advanced settings include maximum depth, child limits, duration, thread count, response size and query parameter handling. Bennetts warns that form processing can cause a crawl to submit contact forms, so it should be turned off where that matters.

The session then shows the spider driven through the ZAP API, with scans started and polled from the web interface and from curl, and option changes reflected in the desktop. The closing section points to the GitHub repositories, the spider package and a wiki page for contributors. Practitioners should tune depth, threads and form handling to fit the target, and use the API alongside the desktop when debugging automation.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Exploring Apps
talks.teaser: Shows ZAP's other ways to discover application content, including imports, form value handling and forced browsing.
talks.summary:
This session in a series of ZAP training sessions covers the ways to find out what an application contains beyond spidering. It starts with importing. URL lists can be loaded from a local file through the desktop or the API, and OpenAPI, GraphQL and SOAP definitions can be imported as well. The SOAP add-on was not on the marketplace at the time because of known problems that were being fixed. A log file importer reads ModSecurity logs and earlier ZAP exports.

The middle of the session covers the form handler, which lets a user set specific values for form fields, such as a search parameter, so the standard spider submits meaningful input instead of default values. Those settings are stored as options, so they can be supplied through configuration at startup. The handler works with the standard spider and with OpenAPI and GraphQL imports, but not yet with the AJAX spider. Definitions that the spider discovers are imported automatically.

Forced browsing is presented as a manual technique. It sends GET requests built from a wordlist to hit well-known directory and file names without crawling, so it can reveal content that nothing links to. The speaker notes that it has no API yet, ships with a default wordlist, and accepts custom lists. Developers are less likely to need it, while testers doing manual penetration tests can use it to find unknown endpoints, then spider or test them from there.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: The Sites Tree
talks.teaser: Coverage of ZAP Deep Dive: The Sites Tree from the conference program.
talks.summary: Simon Bennetts trains StackHawk staff on ZAP's sites tree: deduplicating scan targets by method, path, and parameter names while ignoring most values. He demos contexts for nonstandard separators, structural page parameters, and data-driven nodes to avoid scanning thousands of database-backed URLs twice.

talks.title: ZAP Deep Dive: Ajax Spider
talks.teaser: Shows how OWASP ZAP's Ajax Spider uses real browsers to map modern JavaScript web apps beyond the traditional spider.
talks.summary:
Modern sites often build navigation with client-side JavaScript, so OWASP ZAP’s link-following spider can miss most of the attack surface. Simon Bennetts walks through the Ajax Spider, which drives real browsers through Selenium to click controls, follow DOM changes, and capture traffic that static crawling never sees.

On Juice Shop at port 3000, the standard spider finishes in seconds but leaves a thin site tree—chiefly FTP-related paths—while the Ajax Spider reports hundreds of URLs, WebSocket traffic, and API calls. The demo covers launch paths in the desktop UI, Firefox headless versus visible windows, and how red markers in the site tree distinguish Ajax-discovered assets. Scope handling keeps crawls on-domain; links such as OWASP are intercepted when out of scope. Configuration gets substantial attention: parallel browser windows, crawl depth, maximum crawl states when the DOM changes, duration caps to escape loops, event wait and reload timings for slow pages, optional repeat clicks, form filling, and which HTML elements Selenium may activate.

Practitioners should treat Ajax Spider as a tunable trade-off between coverage and runtime, validate findings in the site tree, and adjust waits and element rules per application. The session also points to the spider-ajax add-on in zap-extensions, ZAP’s Crawljax fork behind browser state tracking, and REST API actions for scan, status, and results—including the limitation of one concurrent Ajax scan and stop-without-pause semantics.

talks.title: Demo at SnykCon
talks.teaser: Demonstrates StackHawk's dynamic application security testing tool in CI/CD, covering findings triage, Jira tickets and Slack alerts.
talks.summary:
Ryan Severance, a founder of StackHawk, presents a demo of the company's dynamic application security testing product. It is designed to run automatically in engineering pipelines instead of as an occasional audit, with the goal of catching security bugs on every pull request so teams can fix them while the code is still fresh.

The walkthrough starts with the scans page and a findings summary. Findings are grouped by type and by state: new findings that would break a build, findings assigned to a Jira ticket, and low-severity items where the risk has been accepted. Each finding links to a cheat sheet and shows the request sent, the full response with the evidence highlighted, and a curl command that recreates the exact request so an engineer can step through the code and debug it. Findings can be sent to Jira with notes attached, after which they no longer count as new. An application view tracks finding trends over time, and integrations with major CI systems, Jira, Datadog and Slack are shown, including Slack notifications that link back to finding details. Scans are configured through a YAML file that covers authentication and what to crawl, including spidering, AJAX spidering for single-page apps, OpenAPI specs and GraphQL introspection. The scanner runs as a Docker command and prints the same findings to the terminal that appear in the web app.

The takeaway is that blocking builds on new findings pushes teams to fix issues before production, while triage states let known backlog items stay tracked without repeatedly failing pipelines. The scanner is built on the open-source ZAP engine, with added features aimed at automation, speed and managing findings.

talks.title: GraphQL Security Testing with StackHawk
talks.teaser: GraphQL Security Testing with StackHawk.
talks.summary: StackHawk co-founders Ryan Sever and Scott Gerlach outline GraphQL security testing: schema introspection, nested query abuse, batching and alias amplification, and authZ gaps that classic web scanners miss. The session positions hawkScan-style CI hooks that treat GraphQL like a first-class attack surface rather than bolted-on REST checks.

talks.title: Hawk Talk: The stackhawk.yml
talks.teaser: Walks through each section of a StackHawk scanner configuration file, using a deliberately vulnerable Django app as the example.
talks.summary:
This short quick-hit episode explains the stackhawk.yml file, the configuration that controls the StackHawk scanner. The presenter starts from the minimal file created by the getting-started flow, which holds only an application ID, an environment name and the host address. The YAML format is strict about indentation, and the app section holds most of the scanning settings. A scan run with just those three values already reports findings from a deliberately vulnerable Django application.

The presenter then adds optional settings one at a time. A risk level describes how important the application is to the business, and an app data type such as PII flags the kind of data it handles. An anti-CSRF parameter is set to Django's middleware token name, and exclude paths keep the scanner away from the admin logout route, which would otherwise end its session. For authentication, the presenter uses the browser inspector to find the username and password field names, a hidden next parameter, a logged-out indicator, and the cookie names to track. A test path that returns a 200 only when logged in confirms the login works. The authenticated scan reaches the admin area and reports more URLs and additional issues, such as missing anti-CSRF tokens and cookie flags on admin pages.

The practical takeaways are to check indentation first when a scan fails, to pull exact form field names from the login page rather than guessing, and to use a known authenticated path to verify that login works before trusting the results.

talks.title: Hawk Talk: Getting Started with StackHawk
talks.teaser: A walkthrough covers signup, API keys, YAML config, Docker-based HawkScan, and viewing first DAST results.
talks.summary:
The session walks through StackHawk’s getting-started flow after login, including Google authorization, collecting name and email, and setting an organization name before the platform outlines the path to a first scan.

The demonstration generates an API key for scanner-to-platform communication, then uses the configure-scan step to name an application, pick an environment, and enter a host such as localhost on port 8020. It downloads a pre-populated StackHawk YAML file for the repository and runs HawkScan via Docker after sourcing environment variables for the API key.

Once the scan starts, the portal waits for HawkScan to probe the running application, then surfaces results for review and troubleshooting. The narrative stresses scanning early and often in development as part of the normal workflow rather than deferring dynamic testing.
